headline: Bank of America fined $1.2 billion. It admits it.
summary: The Treasury fined Bank of America $1.2 billion Tuesday for failing to catch and report money laundering. The bank let more than $5 billion in suspicious activity go unreported, $1 billion of it tied to national security risks. It admitted it willfully broke the law. It is the third-largest penalty in Treasury history.
cover_answer: Making crime money look clean by running it through a bank.
table_question: Is waiting for someone else to spot trouble the same as watching?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: A big bank called Bank of America has to pay $1.2 billion. Its job was to watch for people hiding stolen or secret money, and it did not watch closely enough. A bank is supposed to be like a lifeguard, eyes on the pool the whole time. This one kept waiting for someone else to shout. The grown-ups have it, and your piggy bank is fine.
5-7.why: A lifeguard who waits for a shout. The dollar figure is just big.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, so the script gives them the lifeguard who waits for a shout, a job they have watched from the water. The $1.2 billion is only "a lot," and the crime stays off the card. Expect "is my money okay?" Yes. The bank pays from its own money and says it is fixing it.

8-12.script: Banks have to watch customers' money and report anything that looks like crime. Regulators say Bank of America waited for police and other banks to point things out, like a smoke detector with the battery out, waiting for the neighbours to smell smoke. It admitted it and pays $1.2 billion.
8-12.why: Rule, shortcut, missed money, fine. The dead smoke detector carries it.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out rules and whether they are applied, so the script states the rule, the shortcut regulators found, and the fine. The smoke detector is the mechanism: a watcher that waits for someone else to notice has stopped watching. Expect "who gets the money?" The government. The articles don't say what for.

13-17.script: If a bank admits it willfully broke the law for years, why is the answer a fine? Bank of America pays $1.2 billion, about 17 cents a share, and reports its earnings the next morning. Second: regulators say it put revenue ahead of compliance and let outside tip-offs do its watching. Who was watching the watcher?
13-17.why: A fine a company can price in, and a watcher nobody watched.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the bank admits it willfully broke the law, and the cost is 17 cents a share on results day. The script asks whether that is a penalty or a line item, then who checks the checker, since regulators ordered fixes in 2024. Expect "does anyone go to jail?" Not here. It's civil.

5-7.q: Is my money at the bank gone?
5-7.a: No. The fine comes out of the bank's own money, and the bank says it is fixing the problem.

8-12.a: Making crime money look clean by running it through a bank.

8-12.q: Does the bank go out of business?
8-12.a: No. The fine costs it about 17 cents a share this quarter.

13-17.a: Not in these articles. It is a civil penalty: admit it, pay it.

13-17.q: Why fine them instead of shutting them down?
13-17.a: The articles don't say. Bessent's line: the biggest banks are not above the law.
